report:
**Conclusion: no—current evidence does not show that ginkgo extract reliably relieves tinnitus.** Some individual studies have reported improvement, but the higher-level evidence is inconsistent and too uncertain to establish a meaningful benefit over placebo.

A Cochrane review of four trials (1,543 participants) found no evidence of effectiveness when tinnitus was the primary problem. Its newer review likewise judged the certainty of evidence on benefits and harms versus placebo to be too low to draw firm conclusions. European and American tinnitus guidelines recommend against ginkgo for this purpose.  
Sources: [https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus) · [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383762/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383762/) · [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9668350/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9668350/)

It is also not risk-free: ginkgo can interact with medicines, including anticoagulants/blood thinners, and supplements vary in composition. Discuss it with a clinician or pharmacist before use—particularly if you take medicines that affect bleeding or have surgery planned.  
Source: [https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo)

For persistent bothersome tinnitus, an evaluation for hearing loss and individualized options such as hearing support, cognitive behavioral therapy, and sound-based management has a stronger clinical basis than ginkgo.
